chapter: Asides on character, a piano and Oslo
title: Louis offers his piano for Briggs's daughter
summary: At Louis's home near Versailles he insists the piano is Briggs's for his daughter Barbara, and Briggs forces him to accept 200,000 francs.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Briggs and he had an orchestra --." The person said, "Why sure, Arthur, I know him well, I've been a patron in the place, I can contact him and find out.--," you know. Then Louis told him about how we met way back and worked together and everything else. Then we made a contact and he asked me out to his home, and he lived in very, very fine suburbs of Paris, at Pol Le Deux (??). That's near Versailles. Beaugerval, Beau Crescent, near Versailles. And he invited us to his home and I took my wife and my daughter with me, and he had this piano in the livingroom. He said to me, "Art," he said, "Do you remember." I said, "Sure." He said, "I'm going to play you something. I'm going to play you something you'd probably like to hear one of Chopin's, La Baroque Polonaise." So, I told him, I said, "Look, Louis,

my daughter has just started piano, but we have no instrument." I said, "For the time being, I hope I'll be able to get a piano, because she would not progress unless she has an instrument so she can practice at home."
So, he said, "Art," he said, "You have a piano." I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "Well, it's yours." And I said, "Now look, that's out." He said, "Yes, for your daughter."

He called my daughter over. "Barbara, come over." And she sat at the piano and she started playing tunes that she learned with her teacher, you see, and he said, "Art, when are you going to come and get it, the piano."

I said, "No, that's out." I said, "If you want to sell it to me, if you want to make it a price, I'll accept it," but I said, "But Louis, I couldn't --". "Wonderful piano, reconstructed and everything else."
And he said, 'Well, look, this has been around here, about eight years ago.' And I forced him to take 200,000 francs, which is nothing in comparison --
And I made out a check to his wife whom I'd known at the same time. We were all more or less youngsters together, you see.

And she said, 'Art, I'm going to have a lot of trouble with Lou. Lulu, as we called him, 'Because he won't be satisfied, otherwise.' I said, 'You're going to have to keep your piano, I don't want it.'
So, I said, 'He offered to pay the transportation and everything else.' I said, 'Now, look, that's out.'
